lessons.title: Algebra: Expressions and Equations
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: ALGEBRA uses letters (variables) to represent unknown numbers. An EXPRESSION like 3x + 5 means: three times some number, plus 5. An EQUATION has an equals sign: 3x + 5 = 14. To solve: work backwards — subtract 5: 3x = 9, divide by 3: x = 3. Variables allow us to write general rules that work for any number!
practical_activities: Equation balance scales activity
Algebra tile modelling
Real-world equation word problems

exercises.q: Write an expression for 'five more than three times n'

homework.task: Write equations for: 1) A number doubled minus 7 equals 9. 2) Four times a number plus 3 equals 27. Solve both.

revision.notes: To solve equations: inverse operations. Subtract then divide, or add then divide. Check by substituting.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Negative Numbers and Number Line
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Add and subtract with negative numbers
Apply negative numbers to real contexts
lessons.reading_material: Negative numbers are less than zero. We use them for temperatures below freezing, money owed, and floors below ground. On a number line: ...−4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4... The further left, the smaller the number. −7 < −3 because −7 is further from zero. Adding a negative is like subtracting: 5 + (−3) = 5 − 3 = 2.
practical_activities: Temperature recording on number lines
Lift buttons (B2, B1, G, 1, 2...)
Bank balance positive/negative activity

homework.task: Find today's temperatures of 5 cities. Order from coldest to warmest on a number line.

revision.notes: Negative: less than 0. Number line: left=smaller. Adding negative = subtracting. Multiplying negatives: neg×neg=pos.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Geometry: Coordinates and Transformations
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Plot points in all four quadrants
Reflect shapes in x and y axes
lessons.reading_material: A COORDINATE GRID has two axes: x (horizontal) and y (vertical). Each point has coordinates (x, y). With negative numbers, we have 4 quadrants. TRANSFORMATIONS move or change shapes: TRANSLATION (sliding), REFLECTION (flipping), ROTATION (turning). These are used in computer graphics, architecture, and art!
practical_activities: Battleships on coordinate grid
Reflect shapes over axes
Create symmetrical designs

homework.task: Draw a simple shape on coordinate grid. Translate it by (+3, −2). List new coordinates.

revision.notes: Coordinates (x,y): x=right/left, y=up/down. Reflection in y-axis: change sign of x. Reflection in x-axis: change sign of y.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Persuasive Writing
lessons.subject: English
lessons.reading_material: Persuasive writing tries to change people's minds or behaviour. Features: THESIS (your viewpoint), REASONS (why you're right), EVIDENCE (facts/statistics/examples), COUNTER-ARGUMENT (acknowledge other views), REBUTTAL (knock them down), CONCLUSION (restate thesis strongly). Rhetorical devices: RHETORICAL QUESTIONS ('Don't we all deserve...?'), RULE OF THREE ('it's fast, cheap, and reliable'), REPETITION, DIRECT ADDRESS ('You can make a difference').
practical_activities: Debate: should school uniform be compulsory?
Analyse newspaper editorials for features
Write a letter to the headteacher

exercises.q: A rhetorical question is one that?
In a persuasive essay, why include a counter-argument?
exercises.answer: To show you understand other views and then rebut them, making your argument stronger

homework.task: Write a 3-paragraph persuasive essay: 'All children should learn to code.' Include thesis, reasons, evidence, and conclusion.

revision.notes: PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link. Address counter-arguments. Use emotive language and rhetorical devices strategically.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Biomes of the World
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Describe adaptations of organisms to their biome
lessons.reading_material: A biome is a large region with similar climate, vegetation, and wildlife. Major biomes: tropical rainforest (hot, wet, high biodiversity), desert (hot/cold, very dry), grassland/savanna, temperate forest, taiga (conifer forest), tundra (cold, treeless). Each biome has organisms adapted to its conditions.
practical_activities: Create a biome scrapbook
Compare climate data for different biomes

exercises.q: Which biome has the highest biodiversity?

homework.task: Research one animal adaptation in the Arctic tundra

revision.notes: Biome = region with characteristic climate + plants + animals.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Urbanisation
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Analyse the challenges of rapid urbanisation
lessons.reading_material: Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of people living in cities. Causes: rural-urban migration (jobs, education, services). Rapid urbanisation creates challenges: housing shortages, informal settlements (slums), traffic congestion, pollution. Planned cities aim to be sustainable.
practical_activities: Compare a megacity to a small town using data
Debate: is urbanisation good or bad?

homework.task: Research one megacity and identify two challenges it faces

revision.notes: Urbanisation = more people in cities. Can cause infrastructure strain.

lessons.title: The Industrial Revolution
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Describe the causes and effects of the Industrial Revolution
lessons.reading_material: The Industrial Revolution (1760–1840) began in Britain. Steam engines, factories, and railways transformed production and society. Causes: natural resources (coal, iron), innovations (spinning jenny, steam engine), colonial raw materials. Effects: urbanisation, child labour, pollution, rise of the middle class, global trade expansion.
practical_activities: Compare working conditions in 1800 vs today
Graph population growth during industrialisation

exercises.q: Where did the Industrial Revolution begin?

homework.task: Research the life of a child worker in Victorian Britain

revision.notes: Steam + factories + railways = Industrial Revolution. Britain first. Mixed impact on society.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: What fuelled the Industrial Revolution's machines?

lessons.title: World War I
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Explain the causes of World War I
Describe the main events and outcomes
lessons.reading_material: WWI (1914–1918) had multiple causes: Militarism (arms race), Alliances (Triple Alliance vs Triple Entente), Imperialism (colonial competition), Nationalism. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo triggered the war. New warfare: trenches, poison gas, tanks. Treaty of Versailles (1919) punished Germany harshly, sowing seeds of WWII.
practical_activities: Map the alliances on a world map
Analyse a soldier's letter from the trenches

homework.task: Research the experience of one country during WWI

revision.notes: MAIN causes: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism. 1914–1918.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Quran — Structure and Themes
lessons.subject: Islamic Studies
learning_objectives: Describe the structure of the Quran (surahs, ayahs)
Identify major themes of the Quran
lessons.reading_material: The Quran is the holy book of Islam, revealed to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) over 23 years. It has 114 surahs (chapters) and 6,236 ayahs (verses). Major themes: Tawhid (oneness of Allah), guidance for life, stories of the prophets, the hereafter, and justice. Tajweed is the art of correct Quran recitation.
practical_activities: Explore the structure of the Quran using a physical copy
Identify Makki and Madani surahs
exercises: Name 3 major themes of the Quran
Explain what Tajweed means and why it matters
lessons.homework: Choose one surah, read its meaning, and summarise the message in 3 sentences.

revision.notes: The Quran has been memorised and transmitted unchanged for over 1,400 years — it is the most memorised book in history.

lessons.title: Short Stories — Masters of the Form
lessons.subject: World Literature
learning_objectives: Analyse the structure of a short story
Identify narrative voice and point of view
Compare short stories from different countries
lessons.reading_material: The short story is a tightly crafted form where every word counts. Anton Chekhov (Russia) mastered the 'slice of life' story — characters revealed through small moments. Guy de Maupassant (France) wrote twisty tales with ironic endings ('The Necklace'). O. Henry (USA) popularised surprise endings ('The Gift of the Magi'). Saadat Hasan Manto (Pakistan/India) wrote unflinching stories about partition. The narrative voice can be first person (I), second person (you), or third person (he/she/they).
practical_activities: Read 'The Necklace' (de Maupassant) and debate: who is responsible for Mathilde's fate?
exercises: Summarise 'The Gift of the Magi' in 5 sentences
What is narrative voice? Give an example of each person
What makes a Chekhov story different from an O. Henry story?
lessons.homework: Read one short story by an author from your country or region — write a short review.

revision.notes: Short story = tight structure. Chekhov = subtlety. O. Henry = twist ending. Voice = perspective narrator uses.
revision.tip: Identify the narrative voice in the first paragraph of any story — it shapes everything.

lessons.assessment: Write a 200-word short story with a clear beginning, middle, and end — use first-person narration.
textbook_references: The Necklace and Other Stories — de Maupassant

lessons.title: Navigation and Outdoor Safety
lessons.subject: Survival Skills
learning_objectives: Use a compass to find cardinal directions
Follow trail blazes and map signs
lessons.reading_material: Navigation skills keep you safe in the outdoors. A compass needle always points to magnetic north. Cardinal directions: North, South, East, West. To use a compass: hold level, turn until the red needle aligns with the north marking, then read your bearing. Trail blazes are marks on trees that guide hikers. When hiking: tell someone where you are going and when to expect you back. If lost: STOP (Stop, Think, Observe, Plan). Stay in one place — rescuers can find you more easily.
practical_activities: Outdoor orienteering: use a compass and map to find 5 checkpoints in the school grounds
exercises: Explain how to read a compass bearing
What does STOP mean when you are lost?
Name 4 trail marker types used by hikers
lessons.homework: Walk a 10-minute route near home using only landmarks to navigate — write directions.

revision.notes: Compass = magnetic north. STOP when lost: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Trail blazes guide hikers.
revision.tip: If lost in nature: stay put, signal with a whistle (3 blasts = universal distress).

lessons.assessment: Using a provided map and compass instructions, plot a route from A to B and describe each turn.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Isaac Newton
info_cards.fact: Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation, laying much of the foundation for classical physics.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: A Brief History of Time
info_cards.fact: "A Brief History of Time" by Stephen Hawking (1988) sold over 10 million copies, making it one of the best-selling popular-science books of all time.

info_cards.fact: "Hidden Figures" by Margot Lee Shetterly tells the true story of the African-American women mathematicians whose calculations helped NASA send astronauts into space.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Vincent van Gogh
info_cards.fact: "I dream my painting and then I paint my dream." — Dutch Post-Impressionist painter known for works like The Starry Night and Sunflowers.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Pablo Picasso
info_cards.fact: "Every child is an artist. The problem is how to remain an artist once we grow up." — Spanish artist and co-founder of the Cubist movement, one of the most influential artists of the 20th century.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Frida Kahlo
info_cards.fact: "I paint my own reality." — Mexican painter known for her vivid self-portraits exploring identity and Mexican culture.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Claude Monet
info_cards.fact: "I must have flowers, always, and always." — French painter and founder of Impressionist painting, known for his series of water lily paintings.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Michelangelo
info_cards.fact: "I am still learning." — Italian Renaissance sculptor and painter who created the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and the statue of David.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Johann Sebastian Bach
info_cards.fact: "The aim and final end of all music should be nothing else but the glory of God." — German composer of the Baroque era whose works, including the Brandenburg Concertos, remain central to classical music.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Frederic Chopin
info_cards.fact: "Simplicity is the final achievement." — Polish composer and pianist renowned for his piano works, including nocturnes and polonaises.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Pyotr Tchaikovsky
info_cards.fact: "Inspiration is a guest that does not willingly visit the lazy." — Russian composer known for The Nutcracker, Swan Lake, and his symphonies.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Louis Armstrong
info_cards.fact: "What we play is life." — American jazz trumpeter and singer whose innovations helped shape jazz music in the 20th century.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ella Fitzgerald
info_cards.fact: "The only thing better than singing is more singing." — American jazz singer known as the 'First Lady of Song' for her vocal range and improvisational skill.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Bob Marley
info_cards.fact: "The greatness of a man is not in how much wealth he acquires, but in his integrity and his ability to affect those around him positively." — Jamaican singer-songwriter who helped popularize reggae music worldwide.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ravi Shankar
info_cards.fact: "Music... is a celestial way of expressing... feeling that words cannot." — Indian musician who popularized the sitar and Indian classical music around the world.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Charlie Chaplin
info_cards.fact: "A day without laughter is a day wasted." — English actor and filmmaker best known for his silent-film character, the Tramp.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Audrey Hepburn
info_cards.fact: "Nothing is impossible, the word itself says 'I'm possible'!" — British-American actress and humanitarian known for her films and later work as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Akira Kurosawa
info_cards.fact: "Create with the era. Move with the times." — Japanese filmmaker widely regarded as one of the most influential directors in cinema history.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Hayao Miyazaki
info_cards.fact: "I believe a film, or any story, should have an ending that gives the audience hope." — Japanese animator and director who co-founded Studio Ghibli and created films like Spirited Away.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Maya Lin
info_cards.fact: "I don't think art needs to scream. I think it needs to whisper." — American artist and architect who designed the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Georgia O'Keeffe
info_cards.fact: "I found I could say things with color and shapes that I couldn't say any other way." — American painter known for her large-scale paintings of flowers and the American Southwest.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Diego Rivera
info_cards.fact: "An artist is above all a human being, profoundly human to the marrow of his bones." — Mexican painter famous for his large public murals depicting Mexican history and society.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Yo-Yo Ma
info_cards.fact: "Music happens to be an art form that transcends language." — French-born American cellist celebrated for his virtuosic performances and cross-cultural collaborations.

lessons.title: World Religions and Cultures
lessons.subject: General Knowledge
lessons.reading_material: The world is home to many religions and cultures. Islam (1.8 billion followers): belief in one God (Allah) and the Prophet Muhammad. Christianity (2.4 billion): belief in Jesus Christ. Hinduism (1.2 billion): oldest major religion, many gods and goddesses. Buddhism: founded by Siddhartha Gautama, focused on the path to enlightenment. Judaism: ancient monotheistic religion, basis of Christianity and Islam. Each religion has sacred texts, festivals, and practices that guide its followers.
practical_activities: Cultural showcase: each student shares one fact about their own culture or religion
exercises: List the five major world religions and one key belief of each
What is monotheism?
Name one festival for each of three different religions
lessons.homework: Research a religious festival from a culture different from your own and write a paragraph about it.

revision.notes: Major religions: Islam, Christianity, Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism. Each has unique beliefs and practices.
revision.tip: Respect for other faiths begins with curiosity and understanding.

quiz.question: How many followers does Christianity have approximately?

lessons.assessment: Write a 200-word comparison of TWO world religions, focusing on similarities and differences.

lessons.title: World Cuisines
lessons.subject: Cooking
learning_objectives: Identify dishes from different world cuisines
Adapt a dish for dietary requirements
lessons.reading_material: Food reflects culture, religion, climate, and history. Italian cuisine features pasta, olive oil, and tomatoes. Indian cuisine uses aromatic spices like turmeric, cumin, and cardamom. Japanese cuisine emphasises fresh fish, rice, and umami flavour. Arabic cuisine includes mezze, flatbreads, and slow-cooked meats. Many dishes have been adapted globally — pizza, curry, and tacos are now eaten worldwide. Dietary requirements include vegetarian, vegan, halal, and gluten-free.
practical_activities: Cook or taste a dish from a different culture — discuss its origin and key flavours
exercises: Name one dish from 5 different world cuisines
What makes halal food different?

lessons.homework: Research a traditional dish from a country you've never visited — find its recipe and origin story.

revision.notes: Food = culture + history + geography. Dietary needs: vegetarian, vegan, halal, gluten-free.

lessons.title: Arabic Verb Conjugation
lessons.subject: Foreign Languages
learning_objectives: Conjugate present tense verbs for I/you/he/she
lessons.reading_material: Arabic verbs change form based on subject and gender. Present tense (مضارع): أنا أكتب (I write), أنت تكتب (you write — male), أنت تكتبين (you write — female), هو يكتب (he writes), هي تكتب (she writes). To form a question, add هل at the start: هل تكتب؟ (Do you write?). Negation: add لا before the verb: لا أكتب (I do not write).
practical_activities: Verb conjugation drill: each student takes a verb and conjugates all five forms on the board
exercises: Conjugate 'يذهب' (to go) for all five subjects
Form 3 questions using هل
Negate 3 sentences using لا
lessons.homework: Conjugate 5 Arabic verbs for all persons and write them in a table.

revision.notes: Present tense: أنا أ___, أنت ت___, هو ي___, هي ت___. Questions: هل + verb? Negation: لا + verb.
revision.tip: Write conjugation tables — pattern recognition speeds up learning.

quiz.question: How do you form a question in Arabic?

lessons.assessment: Write 10 sentences using 5 different verbs — include questions and negatives.

lessons.title: Types of Business Ownership
lessons.subject: Business Studies
learning_objectives: Compare sole trader, partnership, and company
Identify advantages and disadvantages of each
Choose a suitable structure for a given scenario
lessons.reading_material: Businesses can be owned in different ways. A sole trader owns and runs the business alone — simple to set up but the owner carries all risk. A partnership is owned by two or more people who share profits and responsibilities. A private limited company (Ltd) has shareholders and limited liability, meaning owners only risk what they invested. Each structure suits different business sizes and goals.
practical_activities: Class debate: which business structure is best for a new café — sole trader, partnership or company?
exercises: List two advantages of a partnership over a sole trader
What does 'limited liability' mean?
Give an example of a business that is a sole trader
lessons.homework: Interview a family member or neighbour who owns a business — ask what type of ownership they have and why.

revision.notes: Sole trader = one owner (all profit, all risk). Partnership = shared. Ltd company = limited liability.
revision.tip: Remember: limited liability protects personal assets if the business fails.

info_cards.title: LAN vs WAN
info_cards.body: A LAN (Local Area Network) connects devices in one building. A WAN (Wide Area Network) connects devices across large distances — the internet is a WAN.

info_cards.title: IP Address
info_cards.body: An IP address is a unique number assigned to every device on a network, like a postal address for computers.

learning_objectives: Identify common cybersecurity threats and defences
lessons.reading_material: A network connects computers to share resources. LAN (local area network) covers one building; WAN covers large areas; the internet is the global network. Data travels in packets. Cybersecurity threats: phishing, malware, ransomware, hacking. Defences: strong passwords, firewalls, antivirus, encryption, two-factor authentication.
